extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; the educated general public interested in manners, morals, and social criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Short, occasional moral and social essays that observe contemporary fashions, follies, and behaviours and offer prescriptive commentary on education, virtue, and public taste. The author both records transient customs and advances principles for proper conduct and critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sweeping generalisations about groups
rubrics_metrics.description: "general Charges against Bodies of Men is the Fault I am writing against."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticises the tendency to ascribe villainy or demon-like qualities to whole parties or peoples (e.g., foreigners calling the English proud, parish rivalries). He urges against irrational contempt for other nations' language, dress, customs, or minds, and against believing every member of an adverse party to be a villain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect diverse talents and occupations
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Necessities of Mankind require various Employments; and whoever excels in his Province is worthy of Praise... Those who are deficient deserve our Compassion, and have a Title to our Assistance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise people are educated differently and have different talents; praise those who excel in their own province, extend compassion to the less able, and avoid denigrating those not bred in the same manner or place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should foster emulation, not vanity or denigration
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is highly proper to instill such a Reverence of the governing Persons, and Concern for the Honour of the Place, as may spur the growing Members to worthy Pursuits and honest Emulation: But to swell young Minds with vain Thoughts of the Dignity of their own Brotherhood, by debasing and villifying all others, doth them a real Injury."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In societies and schools, promote respect for authorities and pride in the institution to encourage honest emulation, but avoid inflating students' self-importance by debasing others. Instead set before youth examples of distinguished persons from less-famed fraternities to broaden ambition and prevent servile imitation and affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct vanity early to cultivate kindness and fair judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: "By such early Corrections of Vanity, while Boys are growing into Men, they will gradually learn not to censure superficially; but imbibe those Principles of general Kindness and Humanity..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early correction of vain behaviours prevents superficial censure later in life and instils general kindness and humanity, making people easier to themselves and beloved by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocate tolerance across religious and political differences
rubrics_metrics.description: "Reflections of this nature have expunged all Prejudices out of my Heart, insomuch that, tho' I am a firm Protestant, I hope to see the Pope and Cardinals without violent Emotions..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate an impartial, tolerant temper that allows one to encounter even those of differing religious or political persuasions without violent emotions; personal conviction need not entail hatred or prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid satirising entire sexes or broad classes
rubrics_metrics.description: "I always hated Satyrs against Woman, and Satyrs against Man; I am apt to suspect a Stranger who laughs at the Religion of _The Faculty_; My Spleen rises at a dull Rogue, who is severe upon Mayors and Aldermen..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from broad satire that attacks whole categories (men, women, professions, office-holders). Targeted criticism is preferable to sweeping ridicule of entire groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record contemporary fashions and follies in occasional essays
rubrics_metrics.description: "I look upon my self as one set to watch the Manners and Behaviour of my Countrymen and Contemporaries, and to mark down every absurd Fashion, ridiculous Custom, or affected Form of Speech that makes its Appearance in the World... Occasional Papers, that take their Rise from the Folly, Extravagance, and Caprice of the present Age."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an essayist, attend closely to transient fashions and social caprices (e.g., petticoats, party-patches, coloured hoods) and publish occasional pieces exposing and correcting these irregularities so that social excesses may be abated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat social improprieties gently but maintain proper distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: "I am for treating the Sex with greater Tenderness, and have all along made use of the most gentle Methods to bring them off from any little Extravagance... I think it however absolutely necessary to keep up the Partition between the two Sexes, and to take Notice of the smallest Encroachments which the one makes upon the other."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reforming fashions or manners (particularly those of women), prefer gentle correction rather than harsh condemnation, but remain vigilant about preserving social or sex distinctions viewed as important by the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute fashions to cultural differences; avoid national derogation
rubrics_metrics.description: "I must observe that this Fashion was first of all brought to us from _France_... I speak not this in derogation of a whole People... Modesty is our distinguishing Character, as Vivacity is theirs..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When criticising a fashion that originates abroad, acknowledge cultural differences and avoid blanket derogation of other nations; explain how a custom may offend one national character while fitting another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer gallantry and noble motive in martial spectacles
rubrics_metrics.description: "We have retained the Barbarity, but lost the Gallantry of the old Combatants. I could wish, methinks, these Gentlemen had consulted me in the Promulgation of the Conflict... This would give the Battel quite another Turn..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If preserving or reviving martial customs (e.g., combative displays), aim to retain the noble, amorous, or gallant motives that ennobled them historically, rather than reducing them to mere barbarous spectacle for money or bloodlust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question public appetite for violent spectacle and pity vs cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is something in Nature very unaccountable on such Occasions, when we see the People take a certain painful Gratification in beholding these Encounters. Is it Cruelty that administers this Sort of Delight? Or is it a Pleasure which is taken in the Exercise of Pity?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflect critically on why audiences enjoy violent spectacles; interrogate whether such delight is cruelty or a perverse exercise of pity and caution against normalising gratuitous violence as entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppose matchmaking for wealth that sacrifices happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The account of 'Sempronia' who arranges matches for money: "The Mothers... had rather see their Children miserable in great Wealth, than the happiest of the Race of Mankind in a less conspicuous State of Life... Sempronia... has no manner of Conscience in the Disparity..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticises social practices where parents or matchmakers prioritize fortune over temperament and happiness; condemns arranging marriages that trade a person's contentment for social or financial gain and exposes the moral emptiness of such manoeuvres (illustrated by Sempronia's cynical arts).
